blindSummary:
This state/province was the first in the country to reintroduce religious criminal law (2000), triggering a cascade of eleven further adoptions by 2002. Activity by its government-backed religious morality-police body is documented here. A 2019 implementation study by an international religious-freedom monitoring commission, using 2017 case data, covers this state/province alongside two others, confirming that the religious-law courts function operationally. No trans-specific incident or carried-out capital sentence is recorded here.

The enacted religious-law framework, the documented morality-police presence and the commission's case evidence together place this state/province at the lower end of the country's religious-law states: its legal basis and morality-police documentation are materially the same as a twin state's, the two differing only marginally, while several other religious-law states/provinces carry far stronger capital-text or carried-out capital-sentence evidence against them.
